1.title: Office Pet Peeves: What Drives Us Crazy
paragraphs: We spend more time with our colleagues than with our families, so it's not surprising that small habits can turn into big irritations. Last month, a recruitment agency in Bogotá surveyed 800 office workers about the behaviour that gets on their nerves the most. The results are funny — and a little worrying.

The number-one pet peeve, mentioned by 62% of the people who answered, was colleagues who talk loudly on the phone. 'It really drives me crazy when someone puts a call on speaker in an open-plan office,' said Juliana, an accountant. In second place were people who eat strong-smelling food at their desks. Tuna and boiled eggs were the foods that people complained about most.

Interestingly, lateness was only fifth. Many workers said they could put up with a colleague who arrives ten minutes late, as long as that person is reliable in other ways. 'What I can't stand is when someone promises to send a report and then forgets,' explained Andrés, a project manager. 'I need people I can trust.'

The survey also asked about positive qualities. The colleagues people look up to most are those who are considerate and trustworthy — people who notice when you're stressed and offer help without being asked. Being funny came third, after honesty and kindness.

So what can you do if a colleague is driving you crazy? Psychologist Marcela Ruiz, whom the agency consulted, recommends speaking to the person privately. 'Most people have no idea that their habits annoy others,' she says. 'It helps when you describe the behaviour, not the person. Say "It's hard for me to concentrate when calls are on speaker", not "You're so rude".'
And if you're into eating tuna at your desk, maybe it's time to try the cafeteria.

1.title: The Neighbour I Look Up To
paragraphs: When our English teacher asked us to write about someone we admire, most of my classmates chose famous people: footballers, singers, scientists. I chose Doña Teresa, the woman who lives in the apartment below mine in Pereira.

Doña Teresa is seventy-three. She's a retired primary school teacher who still gives free maths lessons to the children in our building every Tuesday afternoon. When I was ten and failing fractions, she was the person who saved me. She never got impatient, even when I asked the same question five times.

What I love about her is that she is considerate in a way that most people aren't. It's typical of her to notice when someone is having a bad day. Last year, when my father lost his job, she appeared at our door with a pot of sancocho and didn't ask any questions. She's also completely trustworthy — half the building leaves their keys with her when they travel.

That doesn't mean she's perfect. She has strong opinions, and it gets on her nerves when young people don't say good morning. She once told a delivery man, whose music was too loud, to 'respect the ears of the elderly'. Some neighbours find her a bit strict, but I think it's part of her charm. She just can't put up with bad manners.

I'm into technology, and I want to study software engineering. Doña Teresa doesn't understand much about computers, but she always asks me about my projects. 'Explain it to me like I'm one of my students,' she says.
The people we look up to don't have to be famous. Sometimes they're the ones who live right downstairs.

2.title: Is Learning a Language Online Worth It?
paragraphs: Learning English has become a goal for millions of Colombians, and apps promise to make it easy. But is studying with an app nowhere near as effective as taking classes with a real teacher? We spoke to three learners and an expert.

Manuela, 27, a nurse in Cali, took up English with an app two years ago. 'Using an app is by far the most efficient option for me,' she says. 'I work night shifts, so going to a language school is impossible. Practising for fifteen minutes on the bus is better than doing nothing.' She admits, however, that her speaking hasn't improved as much as her reading.

Felipe, 34, tried apps but gave up after three months. 'Collecting points and badges felt like a game, not like learning,' he explains. 'Taking an online class with a teacher was more expensive, but it was much more worthwhile. I made more progress in two months than in the whole year before.'
Laura, 19, uses both. 'Watching series with English subtitles is my favourite way to learn vocabulary. Talking to a teacher once a week helps me fix my mistakes.'

According to Dr. Andrés Salgado, a language researcher at a university in Medellín, the method matters less than the habit. 'Studying a little every day works far better than studying for five hours once a week,' he says. 'Apps have one big advantage: they're always in your pocket. Their main drawback is that they don't make you speak spontaneously.'

So which is better? The experts agree: learning a language is time-consuming whatever method you choose, and combining methods is the best plan. An app can be similar to a gym: it only works if you actually go — every day.

2.title: My Year Without Sugar
paragraphs: Twelve months ago I decided to give up added sugar. No fizzy drinks, no cakes, no sugar in my coffee — and in Colombia, where tinto almost always comes sweet and every celebration involves a cake, that's not easy. Here's what I learned.

The first two weeks were terrible. I had headaches and I was in a bad mood all the time. Drinking coffee without sugar tasted like medicine. My colleagues thought I was crazy, especially when I refused a slice of my boss's birthday cake. But after a month, something strange happened: fruit started to taste incredibly sweet. A mango was by far the best dessert I'd ever had.

Was it time-consuming? Yes. Reading labels in the supermarket took ages at first. I discovered sugar in bread, sauces, yoghurt and even 'healthy' cereal bars. Cooking at home became essential, and I took up baking with dates and bananas instead of sugar.

The advantages have been enormous. I've lost seven kilos, I sleep better, and my energy is much more stable. I used to feel tired at three o'clock every afternoon; now I feel nowhere near as tired as before. My dentist was impressed, too.
There are drawbacks, of course. Eating out is more difficult, and social events can be awkward. Saying no to my grandmother's arequipe is the hardest thing I've ever done!

Would I recommend it? Not necessarily the strict version. I think reducing sugar is similar to quitting smoking: making progress slowly is more efficient than stopping suddenly. But was it worth it for me? Absolutely. And yes — at Christmas, I had one buñuelo. Just one.

3.title: Emails That Get a Yes
paragraphs: We've all received emails that sound like orders: 'Send me the report today.' Even if the writer doesn't mean to be rude, the message can make people feel uncomfortable. In English, the way you ask for something is almost as important as what you ask for. Here are four techniques for writing requests that people are happy to accept.

1. Soften the request with a modal. Instead of 'Send me the file', try 'Could you send me the file?' or, more formally, 'Would you be able to send me the file by Friday?' The more you need from someone, the softer your language should be.

2. Use an indirect question. 'I was wondering whether you could give me a hand with the presentation' sounds much more polite than 'Help me with the presentation'. Notice the word order: after 'I was wondering whether', the sentence uses normal statement order, not question order.

3. Use 'if' clauses and gerunds. 'Would you mind checking these numbers?' and 'Would it be OK if I left early on Friday?' both give the other person space to say no. And if they do say no, they'll probably use the polite formula 'I'm afraid I can't…'

4. Show appreciation and offer an exit. Phrases like 'I'd really appreciate it if…' and 'I know you're tied up at the moment, so no worries if not' make people more likely to help. Finally, 'Please don't hesitate to contact me if you have any questions' is a classic closing line.

Here's an example. Bad: 'I need the sales numbers right away.' Better: 'Hi Carlos, I hope your week's going well. I was wondering if you could send me the sales numbers by any chance? I know it's a busy week, so I'd really appreciate it. Thanks so much!'
Asking for a favour is a skill. Practise it, and you'll be surprised how often people say yes.

3.title: A Big Favour
paragraphs: Mariana had been staring at her phone for ten minutes. She needed to ask her neighbour, Don Gilberto, for a big favour, and she hated asking people for things. Her flight to Madrid for a job interview was at six the next morning, and the dog-sitter she'd booked had just cancelled.
Finally she knocked on his door. Don Gilberto opened it in his slippers, holding a cup of coffee.

'Good evening, Don Gilberto. I'm really sorry to bother you so late. I was wondering if you could possibly do me a huge favour.' 'Of course, mija. What do you need?' 'Would you mind looking after Lupe for four days? I know it's a lot to ask. I've got a job interview in Spain, and the person who was going to take care of her has cancelled.'

Don Gilberto looked at the small brown dog, who was hiding behind Mariana's legs. 'Four days? Hmm. I'm afraid I'm tied up on Thursday morning — I've got a doctor's appointment. But my grandson could give me a hand. Would it be OK if he took her for a walk that day?' 'Absolutely! I'd really appreciate it. I'll leave you her food, her bed and the vet's number, just in case.'

'Don't hesitate to call me if she gives you any problems,' Mariana added. 'And by any chance, do you know if dogs are allowed in the park on Calle 50?' 'Only on a lead. Don't worry, I know the rules.'

Four days later, Mariana came back with good news: she had got the job. When she went to collect Lupe, the dog didn't want to leave. Don Gilberto laughed. 'If you move to Madrid, I'm keeping her!' Mariana realised she would have to ask him an even bigger favour soon.

4.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
paragraphs: It was a quarter to nine on a Tuesday, and Sebastián was finishing a report for work. His wife was watching the news, and their daughter was doing her homework at the kitchen table. Suddenly, the lights went off. At first, they thought it was just their building, but when Sebastián looked out of the window, he realised the whole neighbourhood was dark.

By the time he had found a torch, his phone was full of messages. Apparently, the power had gone off in half of Barranquilla. Nobody knew why. Meanwhile, the temperature in the flat was rising fast — the air conditioning had stopped, and it was still thirty degrees outside.

The family went down to the street, where most of their neighbours were already sitting on plastic chairs. Someone had brought a speaker that ran on batteries, and before long people were dancing. An old man was telling stories about the blackouts of 1992, when the government had cut the electricity for hours every day.

At about eleven, a neighbour who worked for the electricity company arrived home. He told them that a transformer had broken down after a lightning strike. Engineers were already looking into the problem, but there would be a delay of several hours. In the meantime, everyone should keep their fridges closed.

Sebastián's daughter had fallen asleep on her mother's lap by the time the lights eventually came back, at almost two in the morning. A cheer went up from the street. One witness later told a local radio station, 'It was the best party we've had in years — and nobody organised it.'
The next morning, Sebastián realised he had never saved his report. He had to write it all again.

4.title: Flight Delay Investigation
paragraphs: Incident report: Flight AV-412, Bogotá to San Andrés, 14 March. Prepared by the airline's customer relations department.

Summary: Flight AV-412 was scheduled to depart at 07:10. It eventually left at 13:45, a delay of six and a half hours. This report explains what happened and what we have done to prevent similar problems.

Sequence of events: At 06:30, while passengers were boarding, the pilot noticed a warning light on the control panel. The aircraft had been checked the night before, and no problems had been found. Engineers looked into the warning and realised that a sensor had broken down. Boarding was interrupted, and passengers were asked to return to the gate.

Meanwhile, a replacement part was requested from the airline's warehouse in Rionegro. Unfortunately, by the time the part arrived at 11:20, the original crew had reached their maximum working hours, so a new crew had to be called. In the meantime, passengers received food vouchers.

Several passengers complained that information was not clear. One witness, a passenger who had been travelling with two small children, said that for two hours nobody had explained what was going on. Our investigation confirmed that the gate screens had not been updated and that an alarm had gone off twice in the waiting area by mistake, which caused confusion.

Actions: We have offered every passenger a 50% discount on a future flight. We have also introduced a new rule: during any delay of more than thirty minutes, staff must give passengers an update every half hour.
We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience.

5.title: A Foreigner's Guide to Colombian Etiquette
paragraphs: Colombians are famous for being warm and welcoming, but like every culture, Colombia has unwritten rules that visitors don't always notice. Here's a short guide to help you avoid embarrassing moments.

Greetings. It's the custom to greet everyone when you enter a small shop, a lift or a waiting room — a simple 'buenos días' is expected. In many cities, women greet friends with a kiss on the right cheek, while men usually shake hands. Not greeting people is one of the things that can really offend someone.

Time. Arriving exactly on time for a party is not really expected. If an invitation says eight o'clock, most guests will arrive at nine or later. However, for business meetings and medical appointments, you're supposed to be punctual. Being late to a job interview is something you won't get away with.

Visiting a home. A person who invites you to their house will probably offer you food and drink several times. It's considered polite to accept at least a coffee or a glass of juice. Bringing a small gift, like dessert or flowers, is appropriate but not compulsory.

Paying the bill. In groups of friends, the norm is often to split the bill. But if someone says 'I invite you' ('yo invito'), they are expected to pay for everyone. Offering to pay your part is acceptable, though they will probably refuse.

Things people frown on. Talking loudly about money, criticising someone's family, or making jokes about drug trafficking are things most Colombians find inappropriate. Many people are tired of the stereotypes that films and series show about their country.
Finally, remember that the best etiquette is curiosity. Ask questions, smile, and accept the second arepa. You'll make friends quickly.

5.title: Culture Shock in Japan: A Colombian's Diary
paragraphs: Day 3, Tokyo. I've been in Japan for three days on an exchange programme, and I've already made at least five mistakes. Today I blew my nose on the train and an old lady looked at me as if I'd committed a crime. My host, Kenji, explained later that blowing your nose in public is something people frown on here. I'm supposed to go to the bathroom for that. In Colombia, nobody would notice!

Day 6. The silence on public transport is incredible. On the metro in Medellín, people talk, laugh, sell sweets and play music. Here, talking on your phone on the train is simply not acceptable. Even friends speak in whispers. I'd love to call my mother, but I'll wait until I'm home.

Day 10. Kenji's family invited me for dinner. I'd read about the etiquette, so I knew I was expected to say 'itadakimasu' before eating. What I didn't know was that you should never leave your chopsticks standing up in a bowl of rice — it's a custom associated with funerals. Kenji's grandmother quickly took them out. I wanted to disappear.

Day 15. Something I love: tipping isn't the norm. In fact, it can even offend some people. The service is excellent, but the price is the price. I tried to leave coins in a restaurant and the waiter ran after me to give them back!

Day 21. I'm starting to understand the unwritten rules. Queuing is sacred, and you never get away with pushing in. Shoes come off at the entrance of homes, and there are special slippers for the toilet. Is it strange? A bit. But I find it appropriate somehow — everything has its place.
Kenji is visiting Colombia next year. I'm already preparing him: 'You'll be expected to dance, eat three times more and greet everyone with a kiss.'

6.title: Returns Desk: Five Customer Complaints
paragraphs: Ever wondered what people complain about most? We spent a Saturday morning at the returns desk of a big electronics shop in Bogotá. Here's what we heard.

9:15 — A young man brings back a phone he bought two weeks ago. 'The screen is cracked in the corner and it keeps freezing,' he says. The assistant looks closely. 'I'm sorry, sir, but the warranty doesn't cover broken screens. It looks like it was dropped.' The customer insists it wasn't. The phone needs repairing, and he'll have to pay.

9:40 — A woman returns a coffee machine. 'There's a leak at the bottom. Every morning there's coffee all over my kitchen counter.' This one is clearly faulty. The shop agrees to replace it immediately.

10:20 — An older man has a laptop with a loose hinge. 'The screen keeps falling backwards. I've only had it six months!' A technician checks it and confirms that the hinge needs to be tightened. It's fixed in fifteen minutes, free of charge.

11:05 — A mother returns a pair of wireless headphones. One side doesn't work, and the case is scratched and dented. 'My son is eleven,' she explains with a smile. The assistant suggests buying a protective case next time.

11:50 — The last complaint is unusual. A man brings a white washing machine with a large brown stain on the top. 'It arrived like this,' he says. The delivery company is called in, and the machine needs to be collected and replaced.

What did we learn? Technician Óscar Medina told us that most products don't actually fail — they wear out because of how they're used. 'Keep your receipts, read the warranty, and don't leave devices charging all night,' he advises. 'Batteries really don't like it.'

Third, the handle on the front door is loose. I've tightened the screws twice, but it keeps coming off. I think the lock might be faulty, too, because sometimes the key gets stuck. As you can imagine, this worries me from a security point of view.

Finally, a smaller issue: the washing machine, which came with the apartment, is making a loud noise when it spins. A friend who's a technician took a look and said the belt has probably worn out. It may still be under warranty — do you have the receipt?

I'm happy to let a repair person in any weekday after 5 p.m. or on Saturday mornings. If it's easier, I could also arrange the repairs myself and deduct the cost from next month's rent, as long as you agree.
Thank you for your help. I look forward to hearing from you.

7.title: The River Is Coming Back to Life
paragraphs: For decades, the Bogotá River was known as one of the most polluted rivers in Latin America. Today, thanks to one of the largest environmental projects in the country's history, things are slowly changing.

A major clean-up has been under way since 2016. As part of the project, two large wastewater treatment plants have been built or expanded, and hundreds of kilometres of riverbank have been restored. Right now, new channels are being dug in order to stop factories from dumping chemicals directly into the water.

The effects are beginning to show. According to the regional environmental agency, oxygen levels in some sections have increased significantly as a result of the treatment plants. Birds that had disappeared from the area, such as herons, are being seen again. 'Ten years ago, nobody wanted to walk near the river because of the smell,' says Edilberto Moreno, who has lived in Soacha all his life. 'Now my grandchildren come here to ride their bikes.'

However, the problems are far from over. Due to rapid urban growth, more waste is being produced every year, and illegal connections are still common. The project has also been criticised because of delays and rising costs. Studies are currently being carried out to understand how climate change will affect water levels in the coming decades.

Experts agree that the work is ongoing and that real results will take another twenty years. 'Cleaning a river is not a single action; it's a commitment for a whole generation,' says engineer Lucía Pardo. Each new phase is assessed by an independent committee in order to make sure the money is well spent.
One consequence of the project nobody expected: people are starting to see the river as part of the city again, not as something to hide.

7.title: Why Is Everyone Talking About the Four-Day Week?
paragraphs: Imagine working Monday to Thursday and having every Friday off — without losing any salary. In several countries, this idea is being tested, and in Colombia a few companies have started to experiment with it too.

The largest trial so far was carried out in the United Kingdom in 2022, when around 60 companies reduced their working week for six months. The results have been studied by researchers from several universities. According to their report, most companies decided to continue with the four-day week as a result of the positive experience. Employees reported less stress and better sleep, and many businesses said productivity had stayed the same.

In Bogotá, a software company called Nodo (a fictional name) has been trying the model since last year. 'We didn't do it to be generous,' says its director, Carolina Méndez. 'We did it in order to keep our best people. Thanks to the four-day week, nobody has left the company in twelve months.'

Of course, not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that the model is much harder to apply in hospitals, schools or factories, where someone has to be present. Others worry that people will simply work longer hours on the other four days, which could affect their health. Due to these doubts, many governments are waiting for more evidence.

In Colombia, where a law to reduce the working week from 48 to 42 hours is gradually being introduced, the debate is ongoing. Every change in working hours is being assessed by experts in order to measure its effect on the economy.
What is clear is that the conversation about work is changing. The pandemic showed millions of people that work could be organised differently — and many of them don't want to go back.

8.title: Bus or Bike? Two Commuters, Two Methods
paragraphs: Getting around Bogotá can be exhausting. We asked two commuters how they get to work and why they'd rather do it their way.

Paula, 31, graphic designer. 'I'd rather cycle than take the bus, every single day. I live in Teusaquillo and work in Usaquén, which is about twelve kilometres. By cycling on the ciclorrutas, I get there in forty minutes — the bus can take an hour and a half at rush hour. I'm also really keen on staying fit, so it's two activities in one. The only thing I'd prefer not to do is cycle in heavy rain. On those days, I take a taxi instead of getting soaked.'

How did she start? 'Gradually. I began by cycling only on Sundays, during the ciclovía, when the main roads are closed to cars. Then I worked out a safe route to the office, mostly on bike lanes. Finally, I bought a good light and a raincoat. It was definitely worth doing.'

Jorge, 52, accountant. 'Honestly, I'd prefer to sit comfortably and read. I take TransMilenio from Suba to the centre. It's crowded, yes, but I'd rather be squeezed in a bus than fight with cars on a bike. I'm not keen on exercise, I'll admit it!'

Has he found ways to make it easier? 'Yes, by leaving at 5:45, before the worst traffic. I get a seat and I read a novel a week. I've also cut down on screen time by reading paper books on the bus instead of looking at my phone.'

So which method is better? Transport expert Diana Lozano says it depends on distance and personality. 'The best means of transport is the one you can keep using every day,' she says. 'But for distances under ten kilometres, cycling is usually the fastest option in Bogotá.'

8.title: How I Finally Learned to Save Money
paragraphs: Two years ago, I had a decent salary, no savings and a credit card debt that kept growing. Every month I promised myself I'd save, and every month I failed. Today I have an emergency fund of three months' salary. Here's the method that worked for me.

Step 1: Know where your money goes. I started by writing down every peso I spent for a month. It was painful. I discovered I was spending almost 400,000 pesos a month on food delivery apps. I'd rather not tell you how much I was spending on coffee!

Step 2: Pay yourself first. Instead of saving what was left at the end of the month (which was always nothing), I set up an automatic transfer of 10% of my salary to a separate account on payday. By doing this, I never saw the money, so I never missed it.

Step 3: Cut down on one thing at a time. I'm not keen on extreme budgets — they never last. So I gradually reduced my spending on delivery apps, then on clothes, then on subscriptions I didn't use. I'd prefer to cook on Sundays and take lunch to work than spend 25,000 pesos every day.
Step 4: Use cash for small spending. It sounds old-fashioned, but it works. When you see the notes leaving your wallet, you think twice.
Step 5: Pay off the debt first. I worked out that my credit card was charging me more than 30% interest a year. Paying it off was the best investment I've ever made.
Was it worth doing? Absolutely. Saving isn't a magic trick; it's a habit. And the best means of building a habit is to make it automatic. Start small — even 5% is better than nothing.

9.title: Renovating Grandma's House
paragraphs: When my grandmother moved into a care home last year, my family decided not to sell her old house in Zipaquirá. Instead, my brother and I would renovate it and rent it out. Neither of us had ever renovated anything. Here's what happened.

The first thing we did was get the roof inspected. The inspector told us it needed urgent work, so we got three quotes from local builders. The cheapest estimate was eight million pesos, the most expensive almost fifteen. My brother wanted the cheap one, but our uncle, who is an architect, talked him out of it. 'Why don't you check their previous work first?' he suggested. Good advice: the cheapest builder had terrible reviews.
Next, we had the electrical system checked. The wires were sixty years old! We had new sockets installed in every room and had the old fuse box replaced. It wasn't exciting, but it was necessary.

Then came the fun part. 'How about painting the walls ourselves?' I said. 'It's worth a try.' We spent three weekends painting, and honestly, it looks almost professional. We also got the old wooden floors sanded and varnished. They're beautiful now.
Not everything went smoothly. We kept postponing the garden, and we still haven't got round to fixing the fence. And the gas heater needs to be serviced before winter.

My grandmother came to visit last month. I was nervous — what if she hated it? She walked slowly through every room and then said, 'Have you thought about putting a bench under the lemon tree? Your grandfather would have liked that.' So we went ahead and did it. It's the best thing in the house.
Total cost: twenty-one million pesos. Lesson learned: always get several quotes.

9.title: Car Trouble on the Road to Villavicencio
paragraphs: Camilo had been planning the road trip for weeks. He, his girlfriend Andrea and two friends were going to spend a long weekend in the Llanos. But forty kilometres outside Bogotá, the car started making a strange noise.

'Why don't we stop and check it?' said Andrea. Camilo wanted to keep going, but she talked him into pulling over at a petrol station. A mechanic there, Don Wilson, opened the bonnet and frowned. 'When did you last have the car serviced?' Camilo went red. 'Er… about two years ago.' 'The brakes are almost gone, young man. You can't drive down that mountain like this.'

Don Wilson gave them a quote: 600,000 pesos to have the brake pads replaced and the oil changed. It would take three hours. 'Wouldn't it be better to go back to Bogotá and get it fixed there?' asked Juan, who was worried about the price. 'You could try,' said Don Wilson, 'but I wouldn't even drive back.'
'Let's go ahead with the repair,' said Andrea. 'It's not worth risking our lives to save some money.' Everyone agreed.

While the car was being repaired, they had lunch at a roadside restaurant. 'Have you thought about getting a car inspection before every trip?' Andrea teased. 'I kept meaning to,' said Camilo. 'I just never got round to it.' 'How about making it a rule from now on?' 'Fine. You win.'

Four hours later, they were back on the road. The views of the mountains were spectacular, and the brakes worked perfectly on the steep descent. That night, by the pool in Villavicencio, Camilo raised his glass. 'To Don Wilson — and to Andrea, who's always right.'
'Worth a try,' Andrea said, smiling, 'but I'd prefer a cheaper compliment next time: get the tyres checked before we come home!'

10.title: Colombia in 2050
paragraphs: What will Colombia look like in 2050? Nobody knows for sure, but experts in demography, technology and climate have made some predictions. Here are five of them.

1. An older population. Colombia's birth rate has fallen dramatically during the last fifty years. In 1970, the average woman had about five children; today she has fewer than two. By 2050, one in four Colombians is likely to be over sixty. As a result, the country will have to rethink its pension and health systems.

2. Cities that keep growing. The urban population has grown from about 45% in 1960 to more than 80% today. By then, Bogotá will probably have reached ten million inhabitants. Experts believe that the metro, which has been under construction since 2020, will have become essential by that time.

3. Clean energy. Colombia already gets most of its electricity from hydroelectric plants. In the coming decades, solar and wind energy, especially in La Guajira, will be playing a much bigger role. The government has set the milestone of producing 'net zero' emissions by 2050.

4. Climate challenges. Scientists warn that several glaciers in the Andes are likely to disappear. Some glaciers that existed forty years ago have already melted. Coastal cities like Cartagena will be dealing with rising sea levels.
5. New jobs. Many of today's jobs will have changed or disappeared because of artificial intelligence. On the other hand, new professions that don't exist yet will have been created.

Looking ahead is never easy, and predictions often fail. For the time being, however, one thing seems clear: the decisions that Colombia makes in the next ten years will decide whether the country is on track for a better future.

10.title: My Five-Year Plan
paragraphs: Five years ago, I was working in a shoe shop in Cúcuta, and I had never imagined going to university. Today I'm in the second year of a nursing degree, and I've started to look ahead. My teacher asked us to write about where we'll be in five years. This is my plan.

By this time next year, I will have finished my theoretical courses, and I'll be doing my first hospital placement. I've been working towards this milestone for three years, so I'm excited and a bit nervous.

From 2027 to 2028, I'll be doing my final internship. I'm likely to work night shifts during that period, which won't be easy because I also look after my younger brother. For the time being, my mother helps me, but by then she'll probably have moved back to our family's farm near Pamplona.

By 2029, I'll have graduated — the first person in my family to do so. I'd like to work in a public hospital in Cúcuta for a few years. Our region needs nurses, especially near the border with Venezuela, where thousands of migrants arrived some years ago and the hospitals have been under pressure since then.

Eventually, I hope to specialise in paediatric care. Children's nurses are scarce in Norte de Santander, and I've always been good with kids. In five years' time, I'll be saving for a master's degree, and if everything goes well, I'll be starting it in 2032.

Of course, plans change. Five years ago, I couldn't have predicted any of this. But I've learned that writing down your goals helps you stay on track. Whatever happens, by the time I'm thirty, I'll have built a career that I'm proud of.

11.title: The Job I Turned Down
paragraphs: The moment Santiago opened the email, he knew his life could change. A tech company in Barcelona was offering him a job as a junior developer: a good salary, a visa and a flat for the first three months. He was twenty-six, single and living with his parents in Bucaramanga.

But he didn't accept it right away. Before he replied, he talked to his family. His mother cried. His father said nothing, which was worse. His girlfriend at the time, Melissa, told him she would never leave Colombia. Once he imagined life without them, the offer looked less attractive. After two weeks of sleepless nights, he turned it down.
Three months later, Melissa broke up with him. Six months after that, the local company he worked for closed, and he spent almost a year looking for another job.

'In hindsight, I should have taken it,' Santiago says now, five years later. 'If I had gone to Barcelona, I would have had a completely different career. I blamed Melissa for a long time, but it wasn't her fault. It was my decision.'

Is it all regret? Not quite. Until he lost his job, Santiago had never thought about working for himself. During that difficult year, he started building apps for small businesses in his city. Today he runs a company with eight employees. 'If I hadn't stayed, I wouldn't have met my business partner, and I wouldn't have started this company. Otherwise, I'd be a developer in someone else's team.'
So what's the lesson? 'Don't make big decisions because of fear,' he says. 'And if a plan falls through, look for the door that's opening instead of staring at the one that closed.'
As soon as we finished the interview, he got a call. A client in Madrid wanted to work with him.

11.title: Lessons from a Failed Business
paragraphs: Three years ago, my best friend and I opened a vegan café in Laureles, Medellín. Eighteen months later, we closed it. I've waited until now to write about it, because for a long time I couldn't think about it without feeling sick. But I think the lessons might help someone.

Mistake 1: We didn't research the area. The moment we found a beautiful, cheap space, we signed the contract. We should have spent a few weeks watching who walked past. Once we opened, we realised the street was full of offices that were empty at weekends — exactly when we expected most customers.

Mistake 2: We spent too much before opening. We had the most beautiful furniture in the neighbourhood. In hindsight, we should have bought second-hand chairs and kept the money for the difficult months. By the time we needed money for advertising, there was nothing left.

Mistake 3: We turned down help. My uncle, who has run restaurants for twenty years, offered to look at our numbers. We were too proud. If we had listened to him, we would have seen the problems much earlier.
Mistake 4: We blamed each other. When things went wrong, my friend and I stopped talking honestly. Our friendship almost ended. That was the worst part, and it took us a year to fix it.

Would I do it again? Yes, but differently. I would test the idea first, maybe with a market stall, instead of investing everything at once. Otherwise, you risk losing your savings before you learn anything.

The good news? After the café closed, a bigger deal fell through for another business in the building, and the owner offered us a small kitchen for catering. As soon as we started, orders came in. Sometimes failure is just a detour.

12.title: Why Are Speed Bumps Everywhere?
paragraphs: If you've driven in any Colombian town, you know them well: speed bumps, or 'policías acostados' as they're known here. Some drivers love them, others hate them. But what is their purpose, and why are there so many?

Speed bumps are intended for one simple job: to make cars slow down. They're usually placed near schools, hospitals and residential streets so that pedestrians, especially children, can cross safely. According to road safety experts, a car hitting a pedestrian at 30 km/h is much less likely to kill them than one travelling at 50 km/h. That's the main rationale behind them.

The reason why there are so many in Colombia is partly cultural. Owing to weak enforcement of speed limits, many communities decided to build their own bumps, sometimes without permission. In some villages, residents installed them after a child was hit by a motorbike. 'Nobody listened to us until we did it ourselves,' says one community leader in Cundinamarca.

However, not everyone agrees with this approach. Ambulance drivers complain that bumps slow them down in emergencies. Others point out that badly designed bumps damage vehicles and cause accidents due to sudden braking. Some cities have started replacing them with raised pedestrian crossings, which serve the same purpose but are gentler on vehicles.

Can authorities justify putting a bump in front of every house? Probably not. Transport engineers say that bumps should be used only where there's a clear risk, so that they don't lose their effect. They also recommend painting them bright yellow in order to avoid surprises at night.

Love them or hate them, speed bumps account for a significant reduction in accidents in many residential areas, thereby saving lives — even if they also save a lot of mechanics from going out of business.

12.title: Why We Changed Our School Timetable
paragraphs: Dear families of Colegio Nuevo Horizonte,
As you know, from next term our school day will start at 7:30 instead of 6:30. Several parents have asked us to explain the reason why we made this decision, so we would like to share our rationale.

First, the main purpose of the change is to improve our students' wellbeing. International research shows that teenagers' body clocks are different from adults'. Owing to these biological changes, most adolescents can't fall asleep before eleven at night. With a 6:30 start, many of our students were getting only five or six hours of sleep, and teachers reported that it was very difficult for them to concentrate in the first classes.

Second, we want to reduce the number of late arrivals. Last year, more than 20% of students arrived late at least once a week, mostly due to traffic in the early morning. We hope the later start will help us avoid this problem.

We understand that the new timetable creates difficulties for some families, especially those parents who start work early. For that reason, the library will open at 6:30 for students who need to arrive before classes, so that nobody has to wait outside. Breakfast will also be available, which is intended for students who leave home without eating.

Some of you have asked how we can justify finishing classes an hour later. The extra time at the end of the day will be used for sports and arts, thereby giving students more opportunities to develop their talents.
We will evaluate the change at the end of the year, and we will share the results with you. We believe that well-rested students learn better, and we hope the data will account for our decision.
Yours sincerely, Martha Lucía Cortés, Director

13.title: The Case of the Empty Office
paragraphs: When Patricia arrived at the small accounting office in Chapinero on Monday morning, the door was unlocked and the lights were on. The office's only laptop, which had been on her desk on Friday, was gone.

Her first thought was that someone must have broken in. But there was no evidence of forced entry: the lock wasn't damaged, and the windows were closed. 'Whoever did it must have had a key,' said the police officer who came an hour later. 'That rules out a random burglar.'

Only three people had keys: Patricia, her business partner Ramiro, and the cleaner, Doña Edith. Patricia assumed it couldn't have been Doña Edith; she had worked for them for nine years and was completely trustworthy. Ramiro was on holiday in Santa Marta, so he presumably couldn't have done it either.

Then the officer found something she had overlooked. The security camera in the corridor had been switched off on Saturday at 3:12 p.m. 'Someone who knew the system might have done this,' he said. 'Or someone may have simply forgotten to switch it back on after cleaning.'

The most plausible explanation came that evening. Ramiro called, embarrassed. He had come back from Santa Marta a day early, gone to the office on Saturday to finish some work, and taken the laptop home. He had switched off the camera because it kept beeping. 'I should have told you,' he admitted. 'And I ought to have locked the door. That was pure negligence on my part.'
Patricia was furious, but also relieved. 'You could have sent me a message!' she said. 'Something like this was bound to happen one day, with your memory.'
In the end, she decided to give him the benefit of the doubt. But the next day, she changed the locks — and gave Ramiro the only key that didn't work.

13.title: What Happened to the Ship?
paragraphs: In June 1708, the Spanish galleon San José sank near the Rosario Islands, off the coast of Cartagena. It was carrying gold, silver and emeralds worth billions of dollars today. For three centuries, historians argued about what must have happened that night. The wreck was finally located in 2015 — but some questions remain.

What we know for certain is that the San José was attacked by British warships during a battle. Historical documents show that it exploded and sank in minutes, taking almost all of its 600 crew with it. Only a handful of sailors survived.

But why did it explode? One plausible theory is that a British cannonball must have hit the gunpowder store. Another suggests that the Spanish crew might have blown up the ship deliberately to prevent the British from taking the treasure. Most historians rule out this second idea, since there's no evidence in the survivors' testimonies.

Some researchers believe the Spanish commanders could have avoided the disaster. The fleet had waited in Portobelo for months, and presumably they knew British ships were in the area. They should have waited for an escort, critics say. Leaving without one was a decision that was bound to end badly. Others give the commanders the benefit of the doubt: the fleet had to sail before the hurricane season.

Today, the wreck lies at a depth of about 600 metres. Colombia considers it part of its national heritage, but Spain and other parties also claim it. Underwater archaeologists warn that the site must not be treated simply as treasure: it is also the grave of hundreds of sailors.
One fact can't be overlooked: whatever caused the explosion, the San José remains one of the greatest mysteries of the Caribbean.

14.title: From Bean to Bar: How Chocolate Is Made
paragraphs: Colombia is one of the few countries in the world whose cacao is classified as 'fine flavour'. But how does a bitter cacao bean become the sweet bar in your hand? We visited a small chocolate factory in Santander, which produces around two tonnes of chocolate a month, to find out.

Stage 1: Harvest and fermentation. The cacao pods, which grow directly on the trunk of the tree, are cut by hand. They are opened, and the white, sticky beans are removed. The beans are then placed in wooden boxes, where they ferment for five to seven days. This is the stage that creates most of the flavour.

Stage 2: Drying and sorting. After fermentation, the beans are dried in the sun for about a week. Then they are sorted: broken or mouldy beans are disposed of, and only the best ones are kept. 'Quality control starts on the farm, not in the factory,' says Ana Milena, whose family has grown cacao for three generations.

Stage 3: Roasting and grinding. In the factory, the raw material is roasted in batches of fifty kilos. The beans are then broken into small pieces called 'nibs', and the shells are removed. The nibs are ground for up to three days until they become a smooth liquid.

Stage 4: Tempering and moulding. Sugar is added, and the chocolate is heated and cooled several times. This process, which is known as tempering, gives the chocolate its shine and its 'snap'. Finally, it is poured into moulds.
Stage 5: Packaging. Each bar is inspected, wrapped and labelled with the region where the cacao was grown. Every batch is given a number so that any problem can be sorted out quickly.
The result? A bar that has taken about three months to make — and that you'll probably eat in three minutes.

14.title: Where Does Your Plastic Bottle Go?
paragraphs: Every day, millions of plastic bottles are thrown away in Colombia. Some end up in rivers and the sea, but others start a second life. Here's what happens to a bottle that is recycled correctly in a city like Bogotá.

1. Collection. First, the bottle is separated at home and put in a white bag, which is the colour used for recyclable materials in Bogotá. It is then collected by one of the city's 'recicladores de oficio', the informal recyclers whose work keeps tonnes of plastic out of landfills every day.

2. Sorting. The bottles are taken to a collection centre, where they are sorted by type and colour. Clear PET bottles, which are the most valuable, are separated from green and blue ones. Caps and labels are removed, because they are made of different plastics.
3. Compacting and selling. The bottles are pressed into enormous blocks called bales. These bales are sold to recycling plants, often in batches of several tonnes.

4. Washing and grinding. At the plant, the bottles are inspected again and washed in hot water to remove glue and dirt. Then they are ground into small flakes. Any material that can't be used is disposed of safely.

5. A new product. The flakes are melted and turned into pellets — the raw material for new products. These can be used to make new bottles, clothes, carpets or even school uniforms. Some Colombian companies now produce bottles that are made entirely of recycled plastic.

What can you do? Make sure your bottles are empty and clean, since dirty plastic can contaminate a whole batch. Squash them to save space. And remember that recycling isn't the first step: the best bottle is the one that is never produced. A reusable bottle, which can last for years, is always the better option.

15.title: Report: How to Improve the Neighbourhood Park
paragraphs: Report prepared for the Junta de Acción Comunal, Barrio El Prado, following the residents' survey carried out in March.
Introduction. The aim of this report is to present the main problems in Parque El Prado and to make recommendations for the coming year. A total of 142 residents answered our questionnaire.

Main problems. The most urgent issue, mentioned by 78% of respondents, is lighting. Six of the ten lamps are broken, and many residents, especially women and older people, say they feel unsafe in the park after dark. The second priority is the playground. Some of the equipment is rusty and dangerous; one swing has already been removed after a child was injured. Rubbish was the third issue brought up by residents, particularly at weekends.

Recommendations. First, the broken lamps must be replaced as soon as possible. This should be presented to the local council as a safety problem, not simply a maintenance one. Second, the playground equipment ought to be inspected by a professional, and anything dangerous should be removed immediately. In the long term, a new playground could be funded through the council's participatory budget.

To address the rubbish problem, more bins need to be installed near the football field. It has also been suggested that a monthly clean-up day could be organised with local schools. This is a feasible option that costs almost nothing.

It should be borne in mind that the council's budget is limited, so not all of these changes can be made this year. The committee has got to decide which projects come first. We recommend that the lighting is looked into before anything else.
Conclusion. The park is surely one of the neighbourhood's most valuable spaces. With these improvements, it could become a safe place for everyone.

15.title: The Meeting Nobody Wanted
paragraphs: It was five o'clock on a Friday, and the last thing anyone at the small travel agency in Cartagena wanted was a meeting. But the manager, Liliana, had something urgent to discuss.

'You've all seen the reviews online, haven't you?' she began. Everyone nodded. In the last two months, the agency's rating had fallen from 4.7 to 3.9 stars. 'The main complaint is slow replies. Customers say it takes two days to get an answer. That's not acceptable, is it?'
'It isn't,' said Jhon, who handled the email account. 'But we're only three people, and there are hundreds of messages every week. Something has got to change.'

Liliana nodded. 'So what are your recommendations? Should a chatbot be installed, for example?' Valeria, the youngest member of the team, looked doubtful. 'Surely customers would prefer to talk to a real person, wouldn't they? Our clients are mostly families planning their holidays. They want advice.'
'That's a good point,' said Liliana. 'But we ought to look into it anyway. Maybe a bot could answer simple questions, like prices and timetables, and the complicated ones could be passed on to us.'

Then Jhon brought up another idea. 'What about a priority system? Messages from customers who have already booked should be answered first. New enquiries can wait a few hours.' 'That sounds feasible,' said Valeria. 'And we should bear in mind that the high season starts in December. If we don't address this now, it'll be a disaster.'
By six o'clock, they had a plan: a simple bot would be tested for a month, booked customers would be prioritised, and replies would be sent within twelve hours.
'That wasn't so bad, was it?' said Liliana, smiling. 'No,' said Jhon, reaching for his bag. 'But next time, can we have it on a Tuesday?'

16.title: Looking Back on Ten Years of Running
paragraphs: Ten years ago today, I ran my first five kilometres around the Parque Simón Bolívar. It took me forty-two minutes, and I had to stop and walk three times. I remember thinking I would never be a 'real' runner. Today I want to look back on what I've achieved since then.

In the first year, I set a goal to run a 10K race, and I did it in Bogotá in 2017. A year later I finished my first half marathon. The biggest accomplishment, though, came in 2021, when I completed the Medellín marathon in four hours and five minutes. I cried for the last two kilometres.

So far, I've run nineteen races in six different cities. I've also met my best friends through the running club, and I've raised more than five million pesos for a children's charity by running with sponsors.

Not everything has gone to plan. In 2023 I tried to qualify for the Boston Marathon, which requires a very fast time. I fell short of the target by eleven minutes. I was disappointed for weeks, but I've learned that setting realistic goals is more important than setting impressive ones. I would like to have trained more carefully that year — I got injured because I did too much, too fast.

So what's next? By the end of next year, I'll have run my first trail race in the mountains of the Coffee Region. And by the time I'm fifty, I hope I'll have completed a marathon on every continent. That's my long-term milestone.
In the long run, though, running isn't about medals. It's about the person you become on the way. I'm really looking forward to the next ten years.

16.title: Graduation Speech: What We Have Achieved
paragraphs: Good morning, teachers, families and, of course, my fellow graduates of the class of 2026.

Five years ago, many of us arrived at this technical institute in Neiva without really knowing what we wanted. Some of us had failed at university before. Others had been working for years and thought it was too late to study. I was one of them: a thirty-year-old mother of two who hadn't opened a book since school.

Look at us now. Together we have achieved something remarkable. This class has completed more than 2,000 hours of internships in local companies. Three of our classmates have already started their own businesses, and Andrés, sitting in the front row, qualified for a national robotics competition last year — a first for our institute.

Of course, some days we fell short of our expectations. We failed exams, missed deadlines and sometimes wanted to give up. I would like to have spent more time with my children during these years. But when I look back on everything, I can honestly say that every sacrifice was worth it.

So what's next? Many of you have already set goals. By this time next year, some of you will have found your first professional job. Others will be studying for a degree. In the long run, I believe this class will have changed our region, because we have learned to solve real problems.

My advice? Keep your goals realistic, but not small. Celebrate every milestone, even the little ones. And remember that an accomplishment isn't only the diploma you'll receive today; it's the person you've become to get it.
I'm looking forward to seeing what we all do next. Thank you, and congratulations!
